extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (abstract idea workshop trainees)
extracted.subtask_description: Worksheet for examiner analysis of patent claims under 35 U.S.C. §101 (judicial exceptions/abstract ideas) following the 2014 Interim Eligibility Guidance; walk examiners through identifying the invention, statutory category, whether the claim is directed to an abstract idea (Step 2A), and whether the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more (Step 2B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate worksheet / analyze each claim individually
rubrics_metrics.description: As every claim must be examined individually based on the particular elements recited therein, a separate worksheet should be used to analyze each claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use one worksheet per claim in the SME analysis; do not lump multiple claims together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify what applicant invented (Section I)
rubrics_metrics.description: Review the disclosure to identify what applicant considers as the invention (MPEP 2103(I)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a brief description that does not merely reproduce the claim. The take away should capture the focus of the invention (example: 'invention focuses on scanning and cleaning electronic communications'). This informs later evaluation of additional elements relative to the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construe the claim using broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BRI can be a brief description; avoid merely restating the claim. Use BRI to determine what the claim is 'directed to' in later steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1 — Statutory category check (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claimed invention falls within one of the four statutory categories of invention (process, machine, manufacture or composition of matter) (Step 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose A or B: A = yes (claim is a process/system/product etc.) — continue with SME analysis; B = no — make a rejection of the claim as being drawn to non-statutory subject matter using Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01. If the claim could be amended to fall within a statutory category, consider continuing the SME analysis under that assumption and suggest potential amendment(s); make the assumption clear in the record if a Step 2 rejection is ultimately made.

rubrics_metrics.name: If non-statutory and no amendment possible, conclude SME analysis and proceed
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claimed invention is not one of the four statutory categories and cannot be amended to be, conclude the SME analysis and continue with examination under each of the other patentability requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01 for rejections when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A — Is the claim directed to an abstract idea?
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have found certain concepts to be 'abstract ideas', e.g., fundamental economic practices, certain methods of organizing human activity, ideas themselves (standing alone), or mathematical relationships/formulae. A claim is 'directed' to an abstract idea when the abstract idea is recited in the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assistance in identifying such abstract ideas can be obtained by referring to the case law chart and the 2014 Interim Eligibility Guidance. Determine whether the claim recites a concept similar to those found by the courts to be abstract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A outcome — No (claim not directed to abstract idea) => eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim does not recite a concept similar to those found by the courts to be abstract, conclude SME analysis and continue with examination under other patentability requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An explanation of why the claim is eligible is not necessary in the Office action unless the record would benefit from clarification (for example, to explain interpretation of the claim).

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined analysis when eligibility is self-evident
rubrics_metrics.description: Yes, but the streamlined analysis is appropriate as the eligibility is self-evident, and a full eligibility analysis is not needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use streamlined analysis when the claimed invention 'is not focused on the abstract idea' and 'clearly does not attempt to tie up an abstract idea such that others cannot practice it.' Refer to February 2015 training slides for examples of streamlined analyses. Conclude SME analysis and continue with other examination requirements when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: If directed to an abstract idea, identify the limitation(s) and explain why
rubrics_metrics.description: When Step 2A shows the claim is directed to an abstract idea, identify the limitation(s) in the claim that recite the abstract idea and explain why the recited subject matter is an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fill-in the claim limitations that set forth or describe the abstract idea and provide reasons those limitations are considered abstract (worksheet provides blanks for these).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B — Identify additional elements beyond the abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether there are additional elements (features/limitations/steps) recited in the claim beyond the identified abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose 1: No additional elements => make §101 rejection (use FP 7.05 and 7.05.015) and consider whether disclosure contains elements that could be added to make claim eligible. Choose 2: Yes => list the additional claim elements and continue to evaluate their significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: If no additional elements => §101 rejection and suggest possible amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: If there are no elements in the claim in addition to the abstract idea, conclude SME analysis by making a §101 rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015. Also search the disclosure for elements that could be added to the claim to make it eligible and consider suggesting them to applicant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search for an 'inventive concept' when evaluating additional elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Identifying additional elements and evaluating their significance involves the search for an 'inventive concept' in the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep in mind what applicant invented (Section I) and how that relates to the additional elements. Consider all identified additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance consideration: improves another technology or technical field
rubrics_metrics.description: One reason supporting the significance of additional elements is that they improve another technology or technical field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this consideration when the claim limitations produce a technological improvement beyond the abstract idea itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance consideration: improves the functioning of a computer itself
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional elements that improve the functioning of the computer itself can support finding significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether claim limitations change how the computer operates or improve its performance (e.g., faster computation, less memory usage) rather than merely using a computer as a tool to implement the idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance consideration: applies the abstract idea with/by use of a particular machine (not generic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying the abstract idea with, or by use of, a particular machine that meaningfully limits the application can support eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not a generic computer performing generic computer functions; do not accept mere addition of the words 'apply it' or equivalent; not mere instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer. Consider whether the machine limitation is specific and non-conventional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance consideration: effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements that effect a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing can support that the claim amounts to significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for concrete transformations tying the abstract idea to a real-world change of state or thing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance consideration: adds a specific limitation other than well-understood, routine and conventional activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding a specific limitation beyond what is well-understood, routine and conventional in the field may show significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid characterization that simply appends routine activities at a high level; the added limitation must not be an ordinary generic computer function or other conventional step specified at a high level of generality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance consideration: adds unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application can demonstrate an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These steps must be more than insignificant extrasolution activity, such as mere data gathering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance consideration: adds meaningful limitations beyond linking to a technological environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional elements that amount to more than generally linking the use of the abstract idea to a particular technological environment can support eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely limiting use to the Internet or a computer environment is often insufficient; look for meaningful, concrete limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate additional elements both individually and as an ordered combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider all identified additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether, taken together, they result in the claim amounting to significantly more than the abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document reasons supporting significance; if any elements or combination amount to significantly more, conclude SME analysis as eligible. If not, make a §101 rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic computer components alone do not confer eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Generic recitation of a computer, memory, network, or routine computer functions do not by themselves amount to significantly more than an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example anti-pattern: 'claim amounts to no more than stating create a contract on a computer and send it over a network.' Do not find eligibility based only on generic computer implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement to technology need not be explicit in the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Note that the improvement does not need to be explicitly recited in the claim to support eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An improvement may be shown by how the additional elements integrate the abstract idea into a practical application (e.g., improved performance, reduced memory). Explanations can be included in Office action remarks if helpful to the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: If elements amount to significantly more => conclude eligible and document reasoning if needed
rubrics_metrics.description: If any elements, individually or as a combination, amount to the claim reciting significantly more than the abstract idea, conclude SME analysis and continue with examination under other patentability requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record can be clarified by providing remarks in the Office action explaining why the claim amounts to significantly more (for example: claim recites abstract idea 'x' but amounts to significantly more with additional element 'y' because 'abc'). An explicit eligibility explanation is not necessary unless the record benefits from clarification.

rubrics_metrics.name: If elements do not amount to significantly more => §101 rejection and suggest claim changes
rubrics_metrics.description: If no elements, taken individually and as a combination, amount to significantly more than the abstract idea, conclude SME analysis by making a §101 rejection and continue with other patentability requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015 for the rejection. Identify any disclosure elements that might be added to the claim to make it eligible and consider suggesting such amendments to applicant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use available resources: Quick Reference Sheet, flowchart, case law chart, training slides
rubrics_metrics.description: It is suggested that the worksheet be used with the 2014 Interim Eligibility Guidance Quick Reference Sheet, which includes an overview, the flowchart, and form paragraphs referenced herein.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to the case law chart and court case discussions in the 2014 Interim Eligibility Guidance, and the February 2015 training slides for examples and when a streamlined analysis is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample rejection wording / Form Paragraph guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide suggested template language for a §101 rejection and reasons why the claim is directed to a judicial exception without significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Claim __ is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 because the claimed invention is directed to a judicial exception (i.e., a law of nature, a natural phenomenon, or an abstract idea) without significantly more. Claim __ is directed to ____. The claim does not include additional elements that are sufficient to amount to significantly more than the judicial exception because ____.' Use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015 as appropriate.
